questiontext.text: Fix the minor clauses at some assignment. Major clause c determines predicate p exactly when:

answer.text: p|<sub>c=T</sub> XOR p|<sub>c=F</sub> is true (evaluating with those minor values)

feedback.text: Correct — the two evaluations of p differ, so toggling c alone toggles p.
That would require p true in both cases, meaning c does NOT change p.
Determination is about the two values differing, not about p being true when c is true.

answer.text: c and p have the same truth value

feedback.text: That is not the definition; determination compares p at c=T versus c=F.

generalfeedback.text: With the minor clauses held fixed, c determines p iff evaluating p with c=true and with c=false gives different results, i.e. p|c=T ⊕ p|c=F = true. This XOR test is the operational definition of determination.

questiontext.text: In an active-clause coverage requirement, the major clause is:

answer.text: The clause whose determination of the predicate is being tested

feedback.text: Correct — we focus on one clause at a time and require it to determine p.

answer.text: The clause that appears first (leftmost) in the predicate

feedback.text: Position is irrelevant; the major clause is whichever one we are currently testing.

answer.text: The clause with the most occurrences in the predicate

feedback.text: Frequency does not define the major clause.

answer.text: Any clause that is always true

feedback.text: A constant clause could never determine p; the major clause is the one under test.

generalfeedback.text: Active-clause criteria pick one clause as the major clause (c_i) and require it to determine the predicate; every other clause is a minor clause whose value is chosen to enable that determination.

questiontext.text: When clause c_i is the major clause, the minor clauses are:

answer.text: All the other clauses, whose values are chosen so that c_i determines the predicate

feedback.text: Correct — they are set to let the major clause control the outcome.

answer.text: The clauses that also determine the predicate at the same time

feedback.text: Minor clauses are simply the non-major clauses; they need not determine p.

answer.text: The clauses that are removed from the predicate

feedback.text: They stay in the predicate; only their values are fixed.
Minor clauses may be true or false; the label has nothing to do with their value.

generalfeedback.text: For each choice of major clause, the remaining clauses are the minor clauses. Their values are set (per the criterion's rules) so that toggling the major clause toggles the predicate.

questiontext.text: A clause is said to be active at a given test (assignment) when:

answer.text: It determines the predicate there — flipping it alone would change the predicate's value

feedback.text: Correct — an active clause is one that determines p at that row.

answer.text: It is evaluated to true at that test

feedback.text: Being true is unrelated to being active; an active clause can be true or false.

answer.text: It is the only clause in the predicate

feedback.text: Predicates with many clauses still have active clauses at particular rows.

answer.text: It is masked by the other clauses

feedback.text: A masked clause is the opposite of active — it does not determine p.

generalfeedback.text: A clause is active at a test when it determines the predicate there; the active-clause criteria are named for requiring each clause to be active in the tests that exercise it.

questiontext.text: In General Active Clause Coverage (GACC), the word "General" refers to the fact that:

answer.text: The minor-clause values may differ between the major-clause-true and major-clause-false tests

feedback.text: Correct — GACC is the most permissive about the minor clauses.

answer.text: The minor-clause values must be identical across the pair

feedback.text: That restriction is RACC, not GACC.

answer.text: The predicate must take both values across the pair

feedback.text: That extra correlation requirement is CACC.
That is Combinatorial Coverage.

generalfeedback.text: GACC only requires that the major clause determine p and take both values; it places no constraint linking the minor clauses of the two tests, so they may take any (possibly different) values.

questiontext.text: In Correlated Active Clause Coverage (CACC), what is "correlated" with the major clause changing?

answer.text: The value of the predicate p — it must take both true and false across the pair

feedback.text: Correct — the major clause's flip is correlated with a change in p.

answer.text: The values of the minor clauses, which must stay identical

feedback.text: Requiring identical minor clauses is RACC.

answer.text: The number of true clauses in the predicate

feedback.text: CACC says nothing about counting true clauses.

answer.text: The execution time of the two tests

feedback.text: Correlation here is about truth values, not performance.

generalfeedback.text: CACC requires that, in the pair of tests for each major clause, the predicate p be true in one and false in the other — the change in p is correlated with the flip of the major clause.

questiontext.text: In Restricted Active Clause Coverage (RACC), what is restricted?

answer.text: The minor clauses must hold identical values in the major-clause-true and major-clause-false tests

feedback.text: Correct — RACC pins the minor clauses to the same values across the pair.

answer.text: The number of clauses is restricted to at most three

feedback.text: RACC has no limit on the number of clauses.

answer.text: Only the predicate value is restricted to true

feedback.text: RACC does not fix p to true; the major clause still determines p.

answer.text: The major clause is restricted to being false

feedback.text: The major clause must take both values, not be restricted to false.

generalfeedback.text: RACC restricts the minor clauses to identical values across the two tests of each major clause — the strictest of the three active-clause criteria.

name.text: Test requirements per clause under ACC

questiontext.text: Active Clause Coverage generates, for each clause chosen as the major clause, how many test requirements?

answer.text: 2 — one with the major clause true and one with it false (both determining p)

feedback.text: Correct — each clause yields a true/false determining pair.

answer.text: 1 — a single test where the clause determines p

feedback.text: The clause must be tested both true and false while determining p, so two requirements.

answer.text: 2^n — all combinations of the other clauses

feedback.text: That is Combinatorial Coverage, not ACC.
Each major clause gives exactly two requirements, regardless of n.

generalfeedback.text: For each major clause, ACC requires two tests in which that clause determines the predicate: one with the clause true and one with it false. With n clauses that is 2n requirements (before merging shared tests).

questiontext.text: For predicate p = a ∧ b, clause a determines p exactly when:

feedback.text: Correct — with b true, p equals a, so flipping a flips p.
With b false, p is false regardless of a, so a cannot determine p.
Determination for a depends on the minor clause b, not on a's own value.

answer.text: Never, since it is a conjunction

feedback.text: a does determine p in a conjunction — precisely when the other clause is true.

generalfeedback.text: For a conjunction p = a ∧ b, clause a determines p exactly when the other clause b is true; then p mirrors a.

questiontext.text: For predicate p = a ∨ b, clause a determines p exactly when:

feedback.text: Correct — with b false, p equals a, so flipping a flips p.
With b true, p is true regardless of a, so a cannot determine p.
Determination for a depends on the minor clause b, not on a's own value.
a fails to determine p when b is true.

generalfeedback.text: For a disjunction p = a ∨ b, clause a determines p exactly when the other clause b is false; then p mirrors a. (Dually, in a ∧ b, a determines p when b is true.)

questiontext.text: For a predicate with n independent clauses, the minimum number of tests that can satisfy CACC (MC/DC) is:

feedback.text: Correct — well-chosen tests can be shared across clauses, giving a minimum of n+1.
2n is the upper bound (a fresh pair per clause), not the minimum.
2^n is Combinatorial Coverage, far more than CACC needs.
2 suffices only for Predicate Coverage, not CACC.

generalfeedback.text: Because a single test can serve as the determining test for several clauses at once, CACC/MC-DC for n independent clauses needs a minimum of n+1 tests (and at most 2n).

questiontext.text: The industry criterion MC/DC (as in DO-178C) corresponds most closely to which active-clause criterion?

feedback.text: Correct — generic MC/DC requires each clause to independently affect the outcome, i.e. CACC.
GACC does not require p to change with the clause, so it is weaker than MC/DC.
CoC requires all 2^n combinations; MC/DC needs only about n+1 tests.
PC only checks the whole decision, far weaker than MC/DC.

generalfeedback.text: Generic MC/DC is equivalent to CACC: each clause must be shown to independently affect the decision's outcome. (Strict "unique-cause" MC/DC corresponds to RACC.)

questiontext.text: Active Clause Coverage requires each clause, while it determines the predicate, to be tested both true and false.

feedback.text: Correct — each major clause gets a determining-true and a determining-false test.
ACC's whole point is a true/false pair for each clause while it is active (determining p).

generalfeedback.text: For every clause chosen as the major clause, ACC demands two tests in which the clause determines p: one with the clause true and one with it false.

questiontext.text: GACC, CACC, and RACC together form which family of logic-coverage criteria?

answer.text: The active-clause criteria (each clause must determine the predicate)

feedback.text: Correct — all three require the major clause to be active (to determine p).

answer.text: The inactive-clause criteria (each clause must NOT determine the predicate)

feedback.text: That is the GICC/RICC family, the complement of these.
Those are criteria such as UTPC and CUTPNFP, not the active-clause family.
Combinatorial Coverage is a single criterion, not this family.

generalfeedback.text: GACC, CACC, and RACC are the three active-clause coverage criteria: each requires the major clause to determine (be active in) the predicate, differing only in how the minor clauses and p are constrained.

questiontext.text: A clause that determines the predicate at a given test is called an active clause at that test.

feedback.text: Correct — "active" is exactly the term for a clause that determines p at that assignment.
A determining clause is active; a non-determining (masked) clause is inactive.

generalfeedback.text: Determination and activeness are the same notion: a clause is active at a test precisely when it determines the predicate there. This is why GACC/CACC/RACC are the "active-clause" criteria.

name.text: Minor values for a in (a OR b) AND c

questiontext.text: For predicate p = (a ∨ b) ∧ c, which minor-clause values make clause a determine p?

feedback.text: Correct — then p reduces to a, so flipping a flips p.
With b true, a ∨ b is true regardless of a, so a is masked.
With c false, p is false regardless of a, so a cannot determine p.
Both conditions block a: c false forces p false and b true masks a.

generalfeedback.text: a determines the disjunction a ∨ b only when b = false, and the disjunction determines p = (…) ∧ c only when c = true. So a determines p exactly when b = false and c = true.

name.text: Minor values for b in a AND (b OR c)

questiontext.text: For predicate p = a ∧ (b ∨ c), which minor-clause values make clause b determine p?

feedback.text: Correct — then p reduces to b, so flipping b flips p.
With c true, b ∨ c is true regardless of b, so b is masked.
With a false, p is false regardless of b, so b cannot determine p.
Both conditions block b: a false forces p false and c true masks b.

generalfeedback.text: b determines the disjunction b ∨ c only when c = false, and that disjunction determines p = a ∧ (…) only when a = true. So b determines p exactly when a = true and c = false.

name.text: Minor values for b in (a AND b) OR c

questiontext.text: For predicate p = (a ∧ b) ∨ c, which minor-clause values make clause b determine p?

feedback.text: Correct — then p reduces to b, so flipping b flips p.
With a false, a ∧ b is false regardless of b, so b is masked.
With c true, p is true regardless of b, so b cannot determine p.
Both conditions block b: a false masks b and c true forces p true.

generalfeedback.text: b passes through the term a ∧ b only when a = true, and that term reaches p = (…) ∨ c only when c = false. So b determines p exactly when a = true and c = false.

questiontext.text: For p = a ∧ (b ∨ c) with major clause a, consider the test pair {(a=T, b=T, c=F), (a=F, b=F, c=T)}. Which is the strongest active-clause criterion this pair satisfies for a?

feedback.text: Correct — a determines p in both rows and p differs (T then F), but the minor values (b,c) differ, so it is not RACC.
RACC needs identical minor values; here (b,c) is (T,F) then (F,T), so RACC fails.
It is at least CACC, because p takes both values across the pair.
a determines p in both rows, so at least GACC and CACC are met.

generalfeedback.text: In both rows b ∨ c is true, so a determines p; p is true then false, satisfying CACC (and hence GACC). But the minor values differ ((T,F) vs (F,T)), so RACC is not satisfied. The strongest met is CACC.

questiontext.text: For p = a ∧ (b ∨ c) with major clause a, consider the test pair {(a=T, b=T, c=F), (a=F, b=T, c=F)}. Which is the strongest active-clause criterion this pair satisfies for a?

feedback.text: Correct — a determines p in both rows, p differs, and the minor values (b=T, c=F) are identical across the pair.
The minor values ARE identical here, so RACC (the stronger criterion) is satisfied.
p also takes both values, so CACC and even RACC hold.
A single pair cannot achieve Combinatorial Coverage of three clauses.

generalfeedback.text: b ∨ c = true in both rows so a determines p; p is true then false (CACC); and the minor values (b=T, c=F) match across the pair (RACC). RACC is the strongest satisfied, and RACC subsumes CACC and GACC.

questiontext.text: Why does CACC subsume Predicate Coverage (PC)?

answer.text: Each major clause's pair forces p to be true in one test and false in the other, so p takes both values

feedback.text: Correct — that is exactly what PC requires.

answer.text: Because CACC tests every combination of clause values

feedback.text: That is Combinatorial Coverage; CACC does not test all combinations.

answer.text: Because CACC fixes the minor clauses to identical values

feedback.text: That describes RACC's extra restriction, not why PC is subsumed.

answer.text: Because every clause is made both true and false

feedback.text: That gives Clause Coverage, not Predicate Coverage.

generalfeedback.text: CACC requires p to differ across each major clause's test pair, so p is driven to both true and false — which is precisely Predicate Coverage. (GACC lacks this guarantee, so GACC does not subsume PC.)

name.text: Determination of c in (a OR b) AND c

questiontext.text: For predicate p = (a ∨ b) ∧ c, clause c determines p exactly when:

feedback.text: Correct — when (a ∨ b) is true, p equals c; when it is false, p is false regardless of c.
Then p is false no matter what c is, so c does not determine p.

answer.text: a is true and b is true

feedback.text: c determines p whenever a ∨ b is true, which includes rows where only one of a, b is true.
c cannot determine p when a ∨ b is false.

generalfeedback.text: For a conjunction p = X ∧ c, clause c determines p exactly when the other operand X is true. Here X = a ∨ b, so c determines p when a ∨ b is true.

name.text: Minor values for c in (a OR b) AND c

questiontext.text: For predicate p = (a ∨ b) ∧ c, which condition on the minor clauses makes c determine p?

answer.text: At least one of a, b is true (a ∨ b is true)

feedback.text: Correct — then p equals c.

answer.text: Both a and b are false

feedback.text: Then a ∨ b is false and p is false regardless of c.

answer.text: Both a and b are true only

feedback.text: a=T,b=F (or a=F,b=T) also makes a ∨ b true, so those rows work too.

answer.text: Exactly one of a, b is true

feedback.text: a=T,b=T also enables c to determine p, so it is not "exactly one".

generalfeedback.text: c determines p = (a ∨ b) ∧ c whenever the other operand a ∨ b is true, i.e. whenever at least one of a, b is true (three of the four (a,b) combinations).

name.text: Number of ACC requirements for 3 clauses

questiontext.text: Before merging any shared tests, how many active-clause test requirements does a 3-clause predicate generate?

feedback.text: Correct — 2 requirements (true/false) for each of the 3 major clauses.
Each clause needs a true AND a false determining test, so 2 per clause.
8 = 2^3 is Combinatorial Coverage, not the ACC requirement count.
4 = n+1 is the minimum test count after merging, not the number of requirements.

generalfeedback.text: ACC produces 2 requirements per clause (major-true and major-false, both determining p), so 2 × 3 = 6 requirements. Sharing tests then reduces the actual test count to as few as n+1 = 4.

name.text: Minor values for a in a AND b AND c

questiontext.text: For predicate p = a ∧ b ∧ c, which minor-clause values make clause a determine p?

feedback.text: Correct — then p reduces to a, so flipping a flips p.
Any false clause forces the conjunction false regardless of a.
c = false forces p false regardless of a, so a cannot determine p.
b = false forces p false regardless of a, so a cannot determine p.

generalfeedback.text: In a conjunction, a clause determines the predicate only when every other clause is true. For a ∧ b ∧ c, a determines p exactly when b = true and c = true.

name.text: Minor values for a in a OR b OR c

questiontext.text: For predicate p = a ∨ b ∨ c, which minor-clause values make clause a determine p?

feedback.text: Correct — then p reduces to a, so flipping a flips p.
Any true clause forces the disjunction true regardless of a.
b = true forces p true regardless of a, so a cannot determine p.
c = true forces p true regardless of a, so a cannot determine p.

generalfeedback.text: In a disjunction, a clause determines the predicate only when every other clause is false. For a ∨ b ∨ c, a determines p exactly when b = false and c = false.

name.text: Active clauses at a row of (a AND b) OR c

questiontext.text: For p = (a ∧ b) ∨ c evaluated at a=T, b=F, c=F, which clauses are active (determine p there)?

feedback.text: Correct — flipping b (F→T) makes p true, and flipping c (F→T) makes p true; flipping a leaves p false.
Flipping a (T→F) leaves a ∧ b false, so p stays false; a is not active.
a is not active here: with b false, a ∧ b is false whether a is T or F.
b is also active: flipping b to true makes a ∧ b true, hence p true.

generalfeedback.text: At a=T,b=F,c=F, p = (T∧F)∨F = F. Flip a → (F∧F)∨F = F (not active). Flip b → (T∧T)∨F = T (active). Flip c → (T∧F)∨T = T (active). So b and c are active.

questiontext.text: Correlated Active Clause Coverage (CACC) subsumes General Active Clause Coverage (GACC).

feedback.text: Correct — CACC adds the requirement that p differ across the pair, keeping all of GACC's requirements, so it is at least as strong.
Every CACC-adequate test set is also GACC-adequate, so CACC subsumes GACC.

generalfeedback.text: The active-clause hierarchy is RACC subsumes CACC subsumes GACC. CACC keeps GACC's determination requirements and merely adds the correlation that p change across each pair, so it subsumes GACC.

questiontext.text: Let p = X ∧ c, where X is any subexpression and c is a single clause. Clause c determines p exactly when:

feedback.text: Correct — with X true, p equals c, so flipping c flips p.
With X false, p is false regardless of c.
Determination for c depends on X, not on c's own value.

answer.text: Always, since c is a top-level clause

feedback.text: c is masked whenever X is false.

generalfeedback.text: For a top-level conjunction p = X ∧ c, c determines p exactly when the other operand X is true. Dually, for p = X ∨ c, c determines p exactly when X is false.

questiontext.text: Let p = X ∨ c, where X is any subexpression and c is a single clause. Clause c determines p exactly when:

feedback.text: Correct — with X false, p equals c, so flipping c flips p.
With X true, p is true regardless of c.
Determination for c depends on X, not on c's own value.

answer.text: Always, since c is a top-level clause

feedback.text: c is masked whenever X is true.

generalfeedback.text: For a top-level disjunction p = X ∨ c, c determines p exactly when the other operand X is false. Dually, for p = X ∧ c, c determines p exactly when X is true.

questiontext.text: Why does RACC subsume CACC?

answer.text: Fixing the minor clauses identical while the major clause determines p forces p to take opposite values across the pair, which is exactly CACC's added requirement

feedback.text: Correct — RACC's constraint implies CACC's correlation, and RACC keeps all other ACC requirements.

answer.text: RACC tests all 2^n combinations, which includes every CACC test

feedback.text: RACC does not require all combinations; it uses about n+1 tests, like CACC.

answer.text: RACC drops the determination requirement, making it easier to satisfy

feedback.text: RACC keeps determination; dropping it would make it weaker, not stronger.

answer.text: RACC only applies to two-clause predicates, where CACC is trivial

feedback.text: RACC applies to any predicate.

generalfeedback.text: Under RACC the minor clauses are identical across the pair and the major clause determines p; determination then means flipping only the major clause flips p, so p is true in one test and false in the other — CACC's requirement. Thus every RACC-adequate set is CACC-adequate.

name.text: GACC does not subsume PC — counterexample

questiontext.text: Consider p = a ↔ b (equivalence, true when a and b are equal). Which test set satisfies GACC yet fails Predicate Coverage, showing GACC does not subsume PC?

feedback.text: Correct — both tests give p=true, so PC fails; yet each clause determines p in both, so GACC holds.
Here p takes both values (T then F), so this satisfies PC — not a counterexample.
Here p takes both values (T then F), so this satisfies PC — not a counterexample.
Here p takes both values (T then F), so PC is satisfied — not a counterexample.

generalfeedback.text: For p = a ↔ b each clause always determines p. The set {(T,T),(F,F)} makes each clause both true and false while determining p (satisfying GACC), yet p = true in both rows, so Predicate Coverage is not met. This is the classic proof that GACC does not subsume PC.

questiontext.text: Every test set that satisfies CACC also satisfies Predicate Coverage.

feedback.text: Correct — CACC forces p to be true in one test and false in another of each pair, so p takes both values.
CACC requires p to differ across each major clause's pair, which guarantees Predicate Coverage.

generalfeedback.text: CACC subsumes Predicate Coverage because it requires p to take both truth values across each pair. (By contrast, GACC does not, since GACC lets the minor clauses vary so p can stay constant.)

name.text: Why RACC can be infeasible while CACC is feasible

questiontext.text: Sometimes RACC is infeasible for a clause even though CACC is feasible. The best explanation is that:

answer.text: RACC pins the minor clauses to one identical combination; a constraint among the clauses can forbid that specific combination, while CACC's freedom to use different minor values still allows a valid pair

feedback.text: Correct — the extra restriction of RACC can collide with clause constraints that CACC can sidestep.

answer.text: RACC requires more tests than there are rows in the truth table

feedback.text: RACC needs about n+1 tests, well within the 2^n rows.

answer.text: CACC does not require the major clause to determine p, so it is always feasible

feedback.text: CACC does require determination; that is not the reason.
Infeasible rows are precisely what can make RACC unsatisfiable, not something it ignores.

generalfeedback.text: When clauses are logically coupled, the single identical minor-clause combination RACC demands may be unreachable, whereas CACC can pick two different (each individually reachable) minor assignments. Hence RACC can be infeasible where CACC is feasible.

name.text: Determining rows for a in (a AND b) OR c

questiontext.text: For p = (a ∧ b) ∨ c, in how many of the 8 assignments does clause a determine p?

feedback.text: Correct — a determines p only when b=true and c=false; a is free, giving 2 rows.
6 is the count for c, not a.
a is masked whenever b=false or c=true, leaving only 2 determining rows.
Both a=T and a=F count when b=true, c=false, giving 2 rows.

generalfeedback.text: a determines p exactly when b=true and c=false (so the term a ∧ b passes a through and the disjunction does not mask it). That fixes b and c and leaves a free: 2 of the 8 assignments.

name.text: Determining rows for c in (a OR b) AND (c OR d)

questiontext.text: For p = (a ∨ b) ∧ (c ∨ d), in how many of the 16 assignments does clause c determine p?

feedback.text: Correct — c determines p when (a ∨ b)=true (3 of 4) and d=false (1 of 2), c free (2): 3×1×2 = 6.
That would ignore the d=false condition; only half of those rows qualify.
Recount — 3 (a ∨ b true) × 1 (d false) × 2 (c free) = 6.
c is masked whenever a ∨ b is false or d is true, so far fewer than 12 rows qualify.

generalfeedback.text: c determines c ∨ d only when d=false, and that disjunction determines p only when a ∨ b=true. So c determines p when a ∨ b=true (3 of 4 (a,b)) and d=false, with c free: 3 × 1 × 2 = 6 of 16.

name.text: Determining rows for a in a OR b OR c

questiontext.text: For p = a ∨ b ∨ c, in how many of the 8 assignments does clause a determine p?

feedback.text: Correct — a determines p only when b=false and c=false; a is free, giving 2 rows.
7 is the number of satisfying rows of a ∨ b ∨ c, not the determining rows for a.
a is masked whenever b or c is true, leaving only 2 determining rows.
Both a=T and a=F count when b=false, c=false, giving 2 rows.

generalfeedback.text: In a disjunction a determines p only when every other clause is false. b=false and c=false fixes the minors and leaves a free: 2 of the 8 assignments.

name.text: Determining rows for a in a AND b AND c

questiontext.text: For p = a ∧ b ∧ c, in how many of the 8 assignments does clause a determine p?

feedback.text: Correct — a determines p only when b=true and c=true; a is free, giving 2 rows.
Both a=T and a=F count when b=true, c=true, giving 2 rows.
a is masked whenever b or c is false, leaving only 2 determining rows.
a determines p in only the 2 rows where b and c are both true.

generalfeedback.text: In a conjunction a determines p only when every other clause is true. b=true and c=true fixes the minors and leaves a free: 2 of the 8 assignments.

name.text: Determination condition for a in (a AND b) OR (c AND d)

questiontext.text: For p = (a ∧ b) ∨ (c ∧ d), clause a determines p exactly when:

feedback.text: Correct — b true passes a through the first term, and (c ∧ d) false keeps the disjunction from masking it.
With c ∧ d true, p is true regardless of a, so a is masked.
With b false, a ∧ b is false regardless of a, so a cannot determine p.
Both conditions block a: b false masks a and c ∧ d true forces p true.

generalfeedback.text: a passes through the term a ∧ b only when b = true, and that term reaches p = (…) ∨ (c ∧ d) only when the other term c ∧ d is false. So a determines p exactly when b = true and (c ∧ d) = false.

name.text: Infeasible RACC pair under an implication constraint

questiontext.text: A predicate uses clauses c1: x > 10 and c2: x > 0. A test requirement that needs c1 = true while c2 = false is:

answer.text: Infeasible — x > 10 implies x > 0, so c1 true with c2 false cannot occur

feedback.text: Correct — the clauses are logically coupled, so that combination is impossible.

answer.text: Feasible for some value of x

feedback.text: No x exceeds 10 without also exceeding 0.
No criterion can realize a logically impossible clause combination.

answer.text: Always feasible because the clauses are independent

feedback.text: These clauses are not independent; c1 implies c2.

generalfeedback.text: Because x > 10 logically implies x > 0, the combination c1=true, c2=false is unreachable. Any active-clause requirement (including a RACC pair) that depends on that combination is infeasible and must be excluded.

questiontext.text: A decision has 3 independent clauses. What is the minimum number of tests that can satisfy CACC (MC/DC)?

feedback.text: Correct — n + 1 = 3 + 1 = 4.
6 = 2n is the upper bound, not the minimum.
8 = 2^3 is Combinatorial Coverage.
You need at least n + 1 = 4 tests to show all three clauses independently affect the outcome.

generalfeedback.text: CACC/MC-DC for n independent clauses is achievable with a minimum of n + 1 tests; for n = 3 that is 4.

name.text: What GACC guarantees among PC and CC

questiontext.text: Which statement about GACC and the basic criteria is correct?

answer.text: GACC subsumes Clause Coverage but does not necessarily subsume Predicate Coverage

feedback.text: Correct — every clause is made both true and false (CC), but p may stay constant across a pair (so PC can fail).

answer.text: GACC subsumes both Clause Coverage and Predicate Coverage

feedback.text: GACC need not subsume PC; the equivalence predicate is a counterexample.

answer.text: GACC subsumes Predicate Coverage but not Clause Coverage

feedback.text: It is the other way around: GACC gives CC but may miss PC.

answer.text: GACC subsumes neither Clause nor Predicate Coverage

feedback.text: GACC does make each clause both true and false, so it subsumes CC.

generalfeedback.text: Because each clause is the major clause of a true/false pair, GACC makes every clause take both values, subsuming Clause Coverage. But GACC allows p to remain constant across a pair (e.g. p = a ↔ b), so it does not necessarily subsume Predicate Coverage.

name.text: Determining rows for a in a EQUIV b

questiontext.text: For p = a ↔ b, in how many of the 4 assignments does clause a determine p?

feedback.text: Correct — for equivalence, flipping a always flips p, so a determines p in every row.
a determines p for both values of b, so all 4 rows qualify, not 2.
Determination for a ↔ b does not depend on b, so it holds in all rows.
a always determines p in an equivalence; the count is 4, not 0.

generalfeedback.text: p = a ↔ b equals true when a and b are equal. For any fixed b, flipping a flips p, so a determines p in all 4 assignments. This is why the equivalence gives the GACC-vs-PC counterexample: every row is determining, yet a GACC test set can leave p constant.

name.text: Determining rows for a in (a OR b) AND c

questiontext.text: For p = (a ∨ b) ∧ c, in how many of the 8 assignments does clause a determine p?

feedback.text: Correct — a determines p only when b=false and c=true; a is free, giving 2 rows.
a is masked whenever b=true (a ∨ b already true) or c=false, leaving only 2 determining rows.
6 would be c's count in a different predicate; here a determines p in just 2 rows.
Both a=T and a=F count when b=false, c=true, giving 2 rows.

generalfeedback.text: a determines the disjunction a ∨ b only when b=false, and that disjunction determines p only when c=true. So a determines p when b=false and c=true, with a free: 2 of the 8 assignments.

questiontext.text: Which summary of the active-clause subsumption relationships is completely correct?

answer.text: RACC subsumes CACC subsumes GACC; CACC subsumes PC, but GACC does not necessarily subsume PC

feedback.text: Correct — this captures both the internal ordering and the PC relationship.

answer.text: GACC subsumes CACC subsumes RACC; all three subsume PC

feedback.text: The ordering is reversed and GACC does not necessarily subsume PC.

answer.text: RACC subsumes CACC subsumes GACC; none of them subsumes PC

feedback.text: CACC (and RACC) do subsume PC; only GACC may fail to.

answer.text: All three are equivalent and each subsumes Combinatorial Coverage

feedback.text: They are strictly ordered, and Combinatorial Coverage subsumes them, not the reverse.

generalfeedback.text: The correct picture: RACC ⊇ CACC ⊇ GACC (strongest to weakest). Both RACC and CACC subsume Predicate Coverage because they force p to take both values; GACC does not necessarily, since it can leave p constant across a pair.
